pos: n. (a people or district of the Babylonian empire, named once, among the executioners of God's judgment on Jerusalem)
etymology: Hebrew Qoa', of uncertain meaning; named once in Scripture, at Ezekiel 23:23, where it is generally taken for an Aramaean or Babylonian people or district.
biblical_def: Koa is named once, in Ezekiel's roll of the forces God would bring against Jerusalem: “The Babylonians, and all the Chaldeans, Pekod, and Shoa, and Koa, and all the Assyrians with them: all of them desirable young men, captains and rulers, great lords and renowned, all of them riding upon horses” (Ezekiel 23:23). Nothing more is known of Koa than its appearance in that list; it is generally taken for an Aramaean people or a district under Babylonian rule. The force of the verse is in who sends them. Ezekiel 23 is the parable of the two harlot sisters, and the sentence on Jerusalem is pronounced in verse 22: “Behold, I will raise up thy lovers against thee, from whom thy mind is alienated, and I will bring them against thee on every side” (Ezekiel 23:22). The nations Judah had courted politically are the nations God turns into her executioners, and the armies of Koa and Shoa and Pekod come not as the accidents of imperial history but as the appointed instruments of a holy God. “and I will set judgment before them, and they shall judge thee according to their judgments” (Ezekiel 23:24). The ground of it is named without mercy: “Because thou hast forgotten me, and cast me behind thy back” (Ezekiel 23:35).

And they shall come against thee with chariots, wagons, and wheels, and with an assembly of people, which shall set against thee buckler and shield and helmet round about: and I will set judgment before them, and they shall judge thee according to their judgments.
Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Because thou hast forgotten me, and cast me behind thy back, therefore bear thou also thy lewdness and thy whoredoms.
corruption_summary: Invading armies are explained wholly by imperial ambition, when Ezekiel states plainly that God Himself raised them up and brought them.
corruption_paragraphs: Secular history reads the Babylonian advance as the ordinary expansion of a power, and there is nothing false in the mechanics of that account. What it omits is the verse that governs the chapter: I will raise up thy lovers against thee… and I will bring them against thee. The soldiers of Koa were conscripts of providence. To read the fall of Jerusalem without that sentence is to read the wrong book.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God governs the armies of the heathen as freely as He governs His own people, and that the nations a covenant people court for safety are the nations He may use to chasten them.

pos: n. (a people or district of the Babylonian empire, named once, with Pekod and Koa)
etymology: Hebrew Shoa', of uncertain meaning; named once in Scripture, at Ezekiel 23:23, generally taken for an Aramaean or Babylonian people or district.
biblical_def: Shoa stands beside Koa and Pekod in the single verse that names it: “The Babylonians, and all the Chaldeans, Pekod, and Shoa, and Koa, and all the Assyrians with them: all of them desirable young men, captains and rulers, great lords and renowned, all of them riding upon horses” (Ezekiel 23:23). Of its history we know nothing. What Scripture gives us is a description, and the description is deliberately attractive: desirable young men, captains and rulers, great lords and renowned, all of them mounted. This is the splendour Jerusalem had admired. Ezekiel 23 charges Judah with having doted on exactly such men — on their rank, their cavalry, their reputation — and the judgment is that she shall have them, in the only way the alienated lover ever returns. “And they shall come against thee with chariots, wagons, and wheels, and with an assembly of people, which shall set against thee buckler and shield and helmet round about” (Ezekiel 23:24). The chapter ends where all idolatry ends: “And they shall recompense your lewdness upon you, and ye shall bear the sins of your idols: and ye shall know that I am the Lord GOD” (Ezekiel 23:49). The thing admired becomes the thing that destroys.

corruption_summary: Admiration of worldly splendour is treated as harmless taste, when Ezekiel treats it as the adultery for which a covenant people is given up to the thing it admired.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel does not describe the Babylonian cavalry as ugly. He describes them as desirable young men, captains and rulers, great lords and renowned — and that is the indictment. Judah's sin was not that she was deceived about the glory of the nations but that she preferred it to her God. A church impressed by the world's competence and reputation is committing the same sin at a lower temperature.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God sometimes answers idolatrous admiration by handing His people over to the object of it, and that the end of such a judgment is that they shall know that He is the Lord GOD.

pos: n. (a kingdom summoned against Babylon, named once; the Minni of the Armenian highlands)
etymology: Hebrew Minni, generally identified with the Mannaeans of the Armenian highlands south of Lake Urmia; named once in Scripture, at Jeremiah 51:27.
biblical_def: Minni is named once, in the muster Jeremiah calls up against Babylon: “Set ye up a standard in the land, blow the trumpet among the nations, prepare the nations against her, call together against her the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni, and Ashchenaz; appoint a captain against her; cause the horses to come up as the rough caterpillers” (Jeremiah 51:27). The three kingdoms named are of the northern highlands, and Minni is generally identified with the Mannaeans who lay south of Lake Urmia. Jeremiah is not reporting a coalition that had formed; he is issuing the summons himself, as the LORD's herald, to nations that had not yet moved. Who is actually raising them is stated two chapters earlier in the same oracle: “the LORD hath raised up the spirit of the kings of the Medes: for his device is against Babylon, to destroy it; because it is the vengeance of the LORD, the vengeance of his temple” (Jeremiah 51:11). The summons is repeated: “Prepare against her the nations with the kings of the Medes, the captains thereof, and all the rulers thereof, and all the land of his dominion” (Jeremiah 51:28). And the certainty is grounded not in the strength of the highlanders but in the purpose of God: “for every purpose of the LORD shall be performed against Babylon” (Jeremiah 51:29).

corruption_summary: Prophecy is read as prediction after the fact, when Jeremiah 51 is a summons issued to nations that had not yet stirred.
corruption_paragraphs: The ordinary modern handling of a passage like this is to date it late and read it as history dressed as prophecy. Jeremiah 51 does not read like a report; it reads like an order. A standard is to be set up, a trumpet blown, kingdoms called together, a captain appointed. The prophet commands the Mannaeans of the highlands as a herald commands troops, because the One who sent him had already raised up the spirit of the kings of the Medes.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that every purpose of the LORD shall be performed, and that the fall of a world power may be announced before a single soldier of Minni has saddled a horse.

pos: n. (the camp of Dan, a place behind Kirjath-jearim named from the Danite migration)
etymology: Hebrew Machaneh Dan, the camp of Dan, from machaneh, a camp or encampment; the name stands in the text at Judges 18:12 and in the margin at Judges 13:25.
biblical_def: Mahaneh-dan means the camp of Dan, and it was the name given to a spot behind Kirjath-jearim where the Danite expedition halted on its way north: “And they went up, and pitched in Kirjathjearim, in Judah: wherefore they called that place Mahanehdan unto this day: behold, it is behind Kirjathjearim” (Judges 18:12). The name is a monument to a migration that should never have been necessary. Dan had been allotted an inheritance and had failed to take it: “In those days there was no king in Israel: and in those days the tribe of the Danites sought them an inheritance to dwell in; for unto that day all their inheritance had not fallen unto them among the tribes of Israel” (Judges 18:1). So six hundred armed men went out from Zorah and Eshtaol (Judges 18:11), and what they brought back from the journey was not courage but a stolen priest and a stolen idol: “And the children of Dan set up the graven image: and Jonathan, the son of Gershom, the son of Manasseh, he and his sons were priests to the tribe of Dan until the day of the captivity of the land” (Judges 18:30). A camp named for a tribe became the first stage of a sanctioned idolatry that outlasted the judges and the kings. The Authorized Version also preserves the name in the margin at Judges 13:25, where the camp of Dan is where the Spirit of the LORD began to move Samson.

corruption_summary: The Danite migration is told as a tribal adventure, when Judges presents it as the failure to take a given inheritance and the planting of an idolatry that lasted centuries.
corruption_paragraphs: Readers enjoy Judges 18 as a raid and miss the charge in it. Dan had an inheritance by lot and did not possess it; rather than fight for what God had given, the tribe went looking for easier ground, and on the way it acquired a priest for hire and a carved image. The result is named in the chapter itself: priests to the tribe of Dan until the day of the captivity of the land. Unbelief that looks like enterprise is still unbelief.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a people who will not take the inheritance God assigned will take something else instead, and that what they take will usually be an idol.

pos: n. (a town on the appointed eastern border of Canaan, named twice in one passage)
etymology: Hebrew Shepham, probably a bare or treeless place, perhaps connected with a word for nakedness or barrenness; named at Numbers 34:10 and 34:11.
biblical_def: Shepham is a marker on the eastern boundary God appointed for Israel, and it occurs twice, in two consecutive verses of the same survey: “And ye shall point out your east border from Hazarenan to Shepham” (Numbers 34:10), and then “And the coast shall go down from Shepham to Riblah, on the east side of Ain; and the border shall descend, and shall reach unto the side of the sea of Chinnereth eastward” (Numbers 34:11). The line runs on from there to Jordan and the salt sea, and the chapter closes the circuit with a phrase that is almost a deed of title: “this shall be your land with the coasts thereof round about” (Numbers 34:12). Then Moses states the tenure: “And Moses commanded the children of Israel, saying, This is the land which ye shall inherit by lot, which the LORD commanded to give unto the nine tribes, and to the half tribe” (Numbers 34:13). The land was inherited by lot, which is to say it was distributed by God and not negotiated by men. Shepham's site is unknown, and its obscurity is part of the lesson: the corners of God's gift were fixed in places no modern reader can find, and the gift was no less exact for that.

corruption_summary: Inheritance is conceived as something achieved, when Numbers 34 says the land was inherited by lot and commanded by the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: “This is the land which ye shall inherit by lot” removes the conquest from the category of achievement. The lot is God's instrument precisely because it excludes human contrivance; no tribe negotiated its portion and no family earned its fields. A people who forget this begin to speak of the land as a reward, and from there it is a short way to speaking of salvation the same way.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God measures and assigns the inheritance of His people, and that the exactness of the boundary is the proof of the Giver's care rather than a surveyor's pedantry.

pos: n. (a town of Ephraim built by Sherah, daughter of Beriah, named once)
etymology: Hebrew Uzzen She'erah, the ear or the corner of Sherah, named for its builder; named once in Scripture, at 1 Chronicles 7:24.
biblical_def: Uzzen-sherah is named once, in a parenthesis the Chronicler inserts into the line of Ephraim: “(And his daughter was Sherah, who built Bethhoron the nether, and the upper, and Uzzensherah.)” (1 Chronicles 7:24). The name means the ear or corner of Sherah, and it was called after the woman who built it. That one verse is remarkable on its face. In a genealogy of fathers and sons, a daughter is named, and she is named as a builder of three towns, two of them the Beth-horons which guarded the great pass up from the coastal plain into the hill country — strategic ground that armies fought over for a thousand years. She did this in the shadow of a family grief. Her father Beriah had been named for it: “And when he went in to his wife, she conceived, and bare a son, and he called his name Beriah, because it went evil with his house” (1 Chronicles 7:23). The line continues after her without comment: “And Rephah was his son, also Resheph, and Telah his son, and Tahan his son” (1 Chronicles 7:25). Scripture records a woman's substantial work without fanfare and without apology, in its own good order.

corruption_summary: The honour Scripture gives to a woman's real work is either ignored or conscripted as an argument against the creational order it sits inside.
corruption_paragraphs: Sherah built three towns and the Holy Ghost recorded it, and that record is used in two wrong ways. Some pass over it because a builder in a genealogy ought to have been a son; others make it a lever against the male eldership and headship Scripture establishes elsewhere, as though a woman's competence were an argument about office. Neither handles the verse. The dictionary's position is that God honours women's substantial labour and also appoints order in the church and the home, and that He sees no conflict between the two.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that honourable work is honourable in whoever does it, and that the Chronicler's habit of writing down what others would omit is the habit of a God who keeps accounts.

pos: n. (the mountains of Bether, named once, in the Song of Solomon)
etymology: Hebrew Bather, division or separation, from batar, to cut in two; the Authorized Version margin at Song of Solomon 2:17 gives “of division.” Named once in Scripture.
biblical_def: Bether occurs once, at the close of the second chapter of the Song: “Until the day break, and the shadows flee away, turn, my beloved, and be thou like a roe or a young hart upon the mountains of Bether” (Song of Solomon 2:17). Whether it names a real range or is used for its meaning is disputed in the old commentators, and the Authorized Version itself puts the sense in the margin — of division — from a Hebrew root meaning to cut in two. Read either way, the line is a call across a distance. The bride has just spoken the great mutual possession of the Song: “My beloved is mine, and I am his: he feedeth among the lilies” (Song of Solomon 2:16), and immediately she asks him to come to her over the hills of separation. That is the condition of the church between the advents. The union is already true and already confessed; the presence is not yet full, and the shadows have not yet fled. Earlier in the chapter she had heard him coming: “The voice of my beloved! behold, he cometh leaping upon the mountains, skipping upon the hills” (Song of Solomon 2:8). The book closes with the same petition on her lips, and the mountains are no longer of division but of spices: “Make haste, my beloved, and be thou like to a roe or to a young hart upon the mountains of spices” (Song of Solomon 8:14).

corruption_summary: The Song of Solomon is reduced to an anthology of erotic verse with no reference to Christ and the church, against the whole weight of the Reformed and Puritan reading.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern consensus reads the Song as human love poetry and nothing further, and treats the older Christological reading as pious embroidery. The Reformers and the Puritans read it otherwise, and so does the dictionary: the Song celebrates marriage truly, and marriage is itself the figure Scripture chooses for Christ and His church (Ephesians 5:32). A bride who owns her beloved and still calls him over the mountains of division is the church between the advents, and no reading that cannot hear that has heard the book.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that union with Christ is already real while His presence is not yet full, and that the proper response to the interval is the bride's own petition that He would make haste.

pos: n. (a district or ravine east of Jordan, named once, crossed by Abner in his night retreat)
etymology: Hebrew Bithron, a division or a cleft, from batar, to cut in two; named once in Scripture, at 2 Samuel 2:29.
biblical_def: Bithron is named once, in the account of Abner's night march after the slaughter at Gibeon: “And Abner and his men walked all that night through the plain, and passed over Jordan, and went through all Bithron, and they came to Mahanaim” (2 Samuel 2:29). The name means a cleft or division, and it was evidently a ravine or broken district on the east of Jordan. The day had ended with Joab calling off the pursuit: “So Joab blew a trumpet, and all the people stood still, and pursued after Israel no more, neither fought they any more” (2 Samuel 2:28). Both sides counted their dead; David's house had lost nineteen men and Asahel (2 Samuel 2:30), and Asahel was Joab's brother, which set in motion the blood feud that would end with Abner murdered in a gate. The verse about Bithron is a verse about a long walk in the dark away from a battle a man should not have fought. The chapter that follows states the whole trajectory in one line: “Now there was long war between the house of Saul and the house of David: but David waxed stronger and stronger, and the house of Saul waxed weaker and weaker” (2 Samuel 3:1). God had promised David the kingdom, and the promise worked itself out through years of attrition rather than a single stroke.

corruption_summary: God's promises are expected to arrive by a single decisive stroke, when Scripture records David's accession as years of attrition.
corruption_paragraphs: David had been anointed long before Gibeon and would not sit over all Israel for years yet. The inspired summary is “long war” — not a word anyone would choose for the fulfilment of a divine promise, and exactly the word the Holy Ghost chose. A believer who expects God's word to be kept quickly will mistake a long obedience for a failed promise.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the house of David waxed stronger and stronger by increments, and that God is as faithful in a decade of attrition as in a day of victory.

pos: n. (the place where Hezron died, named once, in the genealogy of Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Kaleb Ephratah, compounding the names of Caleb and Ephratah; named once in Scripture, at 1 Chronicles 2:24.
biblical_def: Caleb-ephratah is named once, as the place where Hezron died: “And after that Hezron was dead in Calebephratah, then Abiah Hezron's wife bare him Ashur the father of Tekoa” (1 Chronicles 2:24). The compound joins the names of Caleb and Ephratah, and the surrounding genealogy explains the pairing: “And when Azubah was dead, Caleb took unto him Ephrath, which bare him Hur” (1 Chronicles 2:19), and later “These were the sons of Caleb the son of Hur, the firstborn of Ephratah; Shobal the father of Kirjathjearim” (1 Chronicles 2:50). The place takes its name from the house that held it. What the verse itself quietly records is a posthumous birth: Hezron dies, and afterward his wife bears him a son who becomes the father of Tekoa, a town that will one day produce the wise woman who pleaded for Absalom and the prophet Amos. Hezron's line had already divided into the three heads Chronicles names: “The sons also of Hezron, that were born unto him; Jerahmeel, and Ram, and Chelubai” (1 Chronicles 2:9), and through Ram that line runs to David and to Christ. A man dies in an obscure place and the covenant goes forward without pausing.

corruption_summary: Genealogy is read as dead record, when Chronicles uses it to carry the covenant line forward through deaths and obscurity to Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: A reader who takes 1 Chronicles 2 for a dry list misses that the chapter is an argument. Hezron dies in a place no one can locate, and the line goes on; through Ram it reaches David, and through David the Son of David. The genealogies are the Holy Ghost's demonstration that the promise was never dependent on any one man's lifespan.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's covenant purpose steps over the graves of the men who carried it, and that a birth after a father's death is as much in His hand as a birth before it.

pos: n. (a place in the north reached by David's census-takers, named once; generally identified with Dan)
etymology: Hebrew Dan Ya'an, of uncertain meaning, perhaps Dan of the wood; named once in Scripture, at 2 Samuel 24:6, and generally identified with the northern Dan.
biblical_def: Dan-jaan is named once, on the route of the men David sent to number Israel: “Then they came to Gilead, and to the land of Tahtimhodshi; and they came to Danjaan, and about to Zidon” (2 Samuel 24:6). The second element is of uncertain meaning, and most take the place for the northern Dan, the traditional limit of the land, under a fuller form of the name. The circuit is the point: the census ran the whole length of the country, and the phrase David himself used for that length was “from Dan even to Beersheba” (2 Samuel 24:2). What makes the chapter hard is its first verse: “And again the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he moved David against them to say, Go, number Israel and Judah” (2 Samuel 24:1). God moved David to a numbering for which David was then justly guilty, which is the plainest Scriptural statement that God's sovereign ordering of a sinful act does not transfer the guilt of it. David's own conscience settles the question of whose sin it was: “And David's heart smote him after that he had numbered the people. And David said unto the LORD, I have sinned greatly in that I have done: and now, I beseech thee, O LORD, take away the iniquity of thy servant; for I have done very foolishly” (2 Samuel 24:10).

corruption_summary: The sovereignty of God over sinful acts is either denied outright or used to excuse the sinner, where 2 Samuel 24 does neither.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Samuel 24:1 says the LORD moved David to number Israel, and the rest of the chapter holds David fully guilty for doing it. Open theism and its relatives resolve the difficulty by denying the sovereignty; the careless resolve it by denying the guilt. Scripture asserts both without embarrassment, as it does at Genesis 50:20 and Acts 2:23. God ordains, and the man who sins in what God ordained has sinned, and his heart will tell him so.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that David's heart smote him and he confessed without once pleading that God had moved him, which is the only posture a believer has in such a case.
